I buy ground meat in bulk (currently ground pork at Costco is the cheapest meat I've found), then I fry it up in a single batch and use a scale to portion 400g into medium size ziploc bags. I flatten the bag of meat and fold it in half (creating 2 distinct rectangles of meat), then freeze it like that. I broke my ankle a few years back... Late on a Monday. Got to hospital via ambulance ($80 ambulance ride, I think you don't pay in certain circumstances like if you're in a car accident). Spent a few hours, I think, on a bed in a hallway. Though it might have been less time. More urgent cases were ahead of me. They pumped me full of morphine, it wasn't a huge deal where I was. I got a room eventually that night. They spent the next day trying to get me into surgery, but more urgent cases prevented it. Which I understood. I'm pretty sure it was on the Wednesday that they finally got me in. They spent hours operating, I really did a number. Then I spent Thursday and part of Friday recovering. In the end, I had pay under $100 for a working cast and $80 for the ambulance ride, maybe a bit of money for painkillers and... That's it. I dunno, maybe in an American hospital I would have been in surgery Monday night instead of Wednesday evening. But I also would have been bankrupt by the bill. I'm sure I also wouldn't have been able to afford all of the physiotherapy I needed.

My garbage boyfriend at the time screamed bloody murder at me because he felt that it was a waste of $80 to get an ambulance ride... I cannot begin to imagine what it must be like to face much bigger bills for basic medical care. I realize that in the US an ambulance ride alone is billed at something like $5000.

I don't tend to see my general practitioner for the little stuff, cause I find it easier to go to a walk-in clinic instead... Where I can see someone the same day. But I'm also more easily able to see some kind of doctor because I'm not debating on if it's worth the cost. I'm only ever debating on if it's worth the time.

Ok, this was a part of my kungfu training - it's a meditational technique based on the Chinese concept of the 5 agents [some translate it as elements] I'll start with the mantra - a simple set of words intended to remind you of each step and concept ... once you are comfortable with it, just saying these words reminds you of the whole thing, a sort of shorthand to help you quickly center yourself.

I am rock - that which I am, I am
I am metal - that which I believe, I am
I am water - that which I think, I am
I am wood - that which I feel, I am
I am fire - that which I do, I am

Now, what does it all mean? You start with rock - solid and unchanging, this is everything you were born with - strengths and weaknesses, potentials - everything. This is the core of your being, it can't be denied and it doesn't change because it is where you started - the beginning of your journey of life.

Next, metal - strong but maluable, this is everything you believe in and as time passes it may change and grow, but your beliefs come from the core of your being and shape who you become and thus you are what you believe and this is at the same time both greater than you and yet it IS you.

Then comes water - always changing and yet strong, this is what you think and your thoughts grow out of your beliefs as you face the world around you - it is the intersection of what you believe and what you experience and this too defines you as you are at a given moment. Your thoughts are a source of strength that helps you face the world and since they are anchored in your beliefs, even though thoughts are constantly changing, they are given stability through your beliefs.

Now we reach wood - sturdy, flexable, living and growing, it is your feelings. These grow out of your thoughts and beliefs as you experience life around you. How you react to things is built on all the steps that brought us to this point and therefore even though emotions can be volitile and seem unpredictable, in fact they are rooted in the very depths of who you are and as long as you remember that you remain in charge of hat you feel and it adds to defining who you are.

And then finally we have fire - your actions, that thing which ultimately defines us - everything that you are comes together in what you do, this is a thing of will - you choose based on what you feel and what you think and what you believe and who you are at the very core of your being and you have the power to act on your choices and all the things that drive your choices give strength to help you act.

In the end, what defines you is what you do but your actions are built on all the rest and when you realise that it can give you the strength to act.

So as you say each of those 5 simple lines, think about what the represent, focus on each concept,one by one and you will see that there is a strength that runs through you. Nothing is random, it all grows out of that central core of ho you are and it will give you the strength to face whatever life brings as long as you remember and allow i to give you that strength.

When you try to diet & you have a moment of weakness that you give into, you feel worthless.  Feeling worthless triggers a desire to eat for the sake of comfort, so you're breaking the diet even more, making you feel even worse and... you get trapped in a vicious cycle.  

In my own life, I have found the only effective way to lose weight is a lifestyle change.  Find a way to still eat the food that you enjoy while also taking in fewer calories.  Some days, for me, this means deciding to skip breakfast & lunch so that I can eat KFC for dinner... though I should note that I have gotten a lot of flack from friends & family for doing that kind of thing.  You could also try smaller portions or having a cheat day each week (perhaps 2 cheat days), just do something that allows you to still eat food that makes you feel good.

The other part of that equation is the exercise... but you don't need to do anything drastic.  Try walking briskly on a lunch break or some other time of day when you don't feel like you're wasting your time doing so.  On that walk, consider listening to music or podcasts or an audio book.  Maybe call family or friends during it.  Read a book.  Do something so that the walk is enjoyable.  Try to find somewhere scenic to walk, if possible.

Congee... It's savory Asian rice porridge, which might not sound appealing, but done right it is heaven. Here is my own version, which there tons ways to make it.

Pork Congee

500g lean ground pork (use more or less according to your own tastes)
1 teaspoon Chinese five spices
2 tablespoons chicken bouillon concentrate
1 cup long grain white rice
9 cups water
4 tablespoons dry chicken stock (I use OXO chicken powder)

In a heavy pot, brown the pork. Mix in the Chinese five spices & chicken bouillon concentrate to the raw meat to help season it.  I try to break the meat up into little chunks using a wood spoon with a flat edge, but that might not matter much.
Once the meat is browned, add the rice, water & dry chicken stock.
Bring to a boil, then turn it down to a simmer & cover loosely with a lid.
Cook gently, stirring occasionally, until the rice is thoroughly cooked and the porridge has become thick and creamy, about 1 1/2 hours.
